title: How Tickling Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why people laugh when tickled. They open with a tangent about spring and a Walmart Black Friday-style incident in which Robert Waller was trampled over a Tickle Me Elmo toy in Fredericton, New Brunswick. They then cover the physiology of touch (nerve endings, nismesis light tickling versus gargoleosis heavy tickling), brain imaging (fMRI, somatosensory cortex, cerebellum, sensory attenuation explaining why we can't self-tickle), historical views (Francis Bacon, Darwin's mood claims, Hecker), ape and rat laughter and tickling research by Jaak Panksepp, why soles of feet and neck are ticklish (Meissner's corpuscles), tickle torture, and theories tying tickling to social bonding. They conclude that the reason for tickle-laughter remains unknown. The episode closes with listener mail from Eric about a Disney College line-standing prank, tied to the earlier riot-control episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and Walmart Tickle Me Elmo incident
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about spring and groundhogs, then discuss Robert Waller, who was trampled and injured at a Walmart in Fredericton, New Brunswick during a Tickle Me Elmo midnight sale. They pivot to the question of why people laugh when tickled.

segments.title: Historical views on tickling and laughter
segments.summary: The hosts note that thinkers such as Francis Bacon and Darwin studied tickling. Darwin's claim that one must be in a good mood to be tickled is said to be disproven. The hosts say the question of why we laugh has not been fully explained.

segments.title: Physiology of touch and tickling
segments.summary: Nerve endings under the skin signal touch. Nismesis is light tickling and gargoleosis is heavy tickling, which alone can induce laughter. Signals pass through the somatosensory cortex and anterior cingulate cortex.

segments.title: fMRI findings and why you can't self-tickle
segments.summary: The hosts explain fMRI as showing correlation, not causation. The cerebellum is less active when a person tickles themselves, which supports sensory attenuation as the reason self-tickling fails. They briefly discuss alien hand syndrome.

segments.title: Socialization, vulnerable spots, and animal laughter
segments.summary: Ticklishness may be learned as protection of vulnerable body areas such as the neck. Apes laugh when tickled, suggesting laughter is ancient. Panksepp's rat studies found ultrasonic chirps and play behavior when rats were tickled.

segments.title: Soles of feet, tickle torture, and social bonding theory
segments.summary: Soles of the feet are ticklish because of Meissner's corpuscles, though the reason is unclear. Tickle torture is discussed. Darwin's theory is that tickling forms social bonds, with the same touch read as attack from strangers and intimacy from loved ones.

segments.title: Conclusion: the reason for tickle-laughter is unknown
segments.summary: The hosts conclude that no one knows why tickling causes laughter. They suggest a future episode on laughter and point to an older article on the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail: Disney line prank
segments.summary: Eric describes a Disney College program prank in which friends stand in a line facing a wall until others join. Josh and Chuck tie it to the earlier riot-control episode and ask for Disney stories.
